analysis.one_liner: Repeals all federal antitrust laws, leaving monopolies and price-fixing unchallenged.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out every major federal antitrust law, including the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act, which are the tools the government uses to break up monopolies, block anticompetitive mergers, and punish price-fixing. It would also strip the Federal Trade Commission of its authority to police unfair methods of competition. The sponsor, Representative Ron Paul, argued that competition is best protected by free entry into markets and that antitrust laws do more harm than good. No other member of the House signed on, and the bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Dominant firms in concentrated industries would gain the most: without the Sherman Act or Clayton Act, mergers to monopoly, price-fixing agreements, and predatory practices could no longer be challenged in federal court, and private antitrust suits by competitors and customers would disappear. The bill's findings argued this would benefit everyone by removing government interference in markets [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, the Antitrust Civil Process Act, and the International Antitrust Enforcement Assistance Act of 1994, and strikes the Federal Trade Commission's ban on unfair methods of competition [S2][S3].

The sponsor's stated purpose is to 'restore the inherent benefits of the market economy,' on the theory that free entry into any market — not antitrust prosecution — is what maximizes consumer welfare, and that the Sherman Act historically was used against rapidly expanding, price-cutting industries while shielding government-created monopoly [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would bear the cost if prices rose after mergers or collusion went unchallenged, since the laws that let the government and private parties sue over monopolization and price-fixing would be gone. Small businesses and new entrants would also lose the legal protection antitrust provides against exclusionary conduct by dominant rivals.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate the only federal statutes against monopolization, anticompetitive mergers, and price-fixing, removing both government enforcement and private lawsuits under those laws [S2][S3].

Repeal would leave no federal check on dominant firms acquiring or excluding rivals; the standard economic rationale for antitrust is that without it, collusion and monopoly pricing raise prices and reduce output for consumers. This is a general feature of how antitrust law works, not a claim found in the bill's own text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's case rests on the argument that antitrust laws punish genuinely competitive, price-cutting firms and that 'free entry' alone disciplines markets [S3]. The cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge is the complete loss of legal remedies against price-fixing and monopoly consolidation — the conduct these statutes were written to reach — with no replacement mechanism in the bill itself. Because the bill repeals the entire framework rather than reforming specific doctrines, the downside risk falls entirely on consumers and smaller firms.

outcome.mechanism: It never went anywhere: after being referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the bill sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Representative Ron Paul introduced the bill on May 13, 1999, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
No other representative signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The only action after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on May 18, 1999 [S5].
The bill was never reported out of committee, so it never reached the House floor for a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and businesses that rely on antitrust law came out ahead: the existing framework stayed intact because the bill never advanced. Dominant firms simply kept operating under the rules they already faced, and no coalition formed to change them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers, since antitrust laws stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal all federal antitrust laws and delivered introductory remarks on the floor [S1][S3][S5].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress [S1][S5].

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member cosponsored, so the partisan shape of opinion on the bill was never tested; the sponsor was a Republican with no support from either party.

industries.note: Repealing the Sherman and Clayton Acts would remove the threat of government suits and private damages actions for monopolization, price-fixing, and anticompetitive mergers [S2][S3]. Consumers would pay through higher prices and less choice if that happened.
Antitrust law is one of the few legal tools small firms and new entrants can use against exclusionary conduct by dominant rivals; the bill would take that away along with government enforcement [S3].

industries.industry: Antitrust bar and enforcement agencies (DOJ Antitrust Division, FTC)
industries.note: The bill repeals the statutes these agencies enforce and strips the FTC's Section 5 competition authority, eliminating their core mission and much of the private antitrust litigation practice [S2][S3].
